title: Israel before the kings: Moses, Joshua and the judges

intro.text: After Joshua's generation died, Judges describes a repeated pattern: Israel served other gods, the LORD gave them into the hands of oppressors, he raised up judges who delivered them, and when each judge died they turned back.
The book ends: "In those days there was no king in Israel: every man did that which was right in his own eyes."

Our count of the numbers in Judges 3–16: 111 years of oppression (8, 18, 20, 7, 18 and 40), 200 years of rest (40, 80, 40 and 40), Abimelech's 3 years, and 96 years in which judges are said to have judged (23, 22, 6, 7, 10, 8 and Samson's 20). That makes 410 years, or 390 if Samson's 20 fall inside the Philistine 40. Eli's 40 years follow in 1 Samuel 4:18.

Scripture gives three wider totals: Jephthah says Israel had held the land east of the Jordan "three hundred years"; Solomon began the temple "in the four hundred and eightieth year" after the Exodus; and in the KJV of Acts 13:20 Paul says God gave judges "about the space of four hundred and fifty years".
Text note: the KJV follows a Greek text that places the 450 years with the judges. Keil reports that the oldest manuscripts known to him read the verse so that the 450 years come before the judges.

Because the order and overlaps of the judges are uncertain, these pages give no year BC for any judge. Each page shows Scripture's own numbers, and the different ways of adding them up are set out as views.
Outside the Bible, a victory hymn of Pharaoh Merneptah says "Israel is desolated, his seed is not". Breasted (1906) called it the earliest mention of Israel then known. It names no judge.

Where the whole period sits depends on the date of the Exodus: about 1448 BC if the 480 years of 1 Kings 6:1 are counted back (Mack, 1915), or in the 13th century BC if the Exodus fell under Merenptah (Driver, 1911).

rulers.name: Moses
rulers.title: Leader of Israel, lawgiver and prophet
rulers.tagline: Forty years leading Israel from Egypt to the plains of Moab.

death.text: Moses died in the land of Moab at 120 years old, "according to the word of the LORD", and Israel wept for him thirty days.

burial.text: And he buried him in a valley in the land of Moab, over against Beth-peor: but no man knoweth of his sepulchre unto this day.

reign.text: Forty years, from the Exodus to the plains of Moab

dates.label: Scripture's own numbers
dates.note: Scripture gives Moses' ages (80 when he spoke to Pharaoh, 120 at his death) and forty years of leadership, but no year BC. The two dates below are scholars' reconstructions of the Exodus, not of Moses' life.

dates.label: Early Exodus (1 Kings 6:1 counted back)
dates.note: Mack (ISBE, 1915) counts the 480 years of 1 Kings 6:1 back from Solomon's temple and puts the Exodus about 1448 BC.

dates.label: Exodus under Merenptah
dates.note: Driver (1911) places the Exodus under Pharaoh Merenptah; these are that pharaoh's years on Petrie's dates, not the years of Moses' leadership.

verdictNotes.text: At Meribah Moses struck the rock and said "must we fetch you water"; God told him he would not bring the people into the land.
The Psalms say "it went ill with Moses for their sakes", because "he spake unadvisedly with his lips".

scriptureSays.text: Stephen calls him the man whom Israel refused as "a ruler and a judge", and whom God sent "to be a ruler and a deliverer".
"Now the man Moses was very meek, above all the men which were upon the face of the earth."
God speaks with Moses "mouth to mouth", and calls him faithful "in all mine house".
"There arose not a prophet since in Israel like unto Moses, whom the LORD knew face to face."
Moses stood "in the breach" to turn God's wrath from the people.
Later Scripture remembers the Exodus as led "by the hand of Moses and Aaron", with Miriam sent before the people too.
"The law was given by Moses."

accession.text: Forty years before his call, a Hebrew had refused him: "Who made thee a prince and a judge over us?"
At Horeb, from the burning bush, God sent him: "I will send thee unto Pharaoh, that thou mayest bring forth my people".
Moses said he was "slow of speech"; God gave him Aaron as spokesman: "thou shalt be to him instead of God".
Moses and Aaron gathered the elders; the people believed and worshipped.
He was eighty when he and Aaron spoke to Pharaoh.

claim.text: On the night of the Passover the LORD brought Israel out of Egypt "by their armies", as he had commanded Moses and Aaron.
After the sea, the people "believed the LORD, and his servant Moses".
Joshua fought Amalek while Moses held up his hands on the hill, with Aaron and Hur holding them steady; Moses built the altar "Jehovah-nissi".
Moses judged the people alone from morning to evening; on Jethro's advice he chose able men as rulers of thousands, hundreds, fifties and tens, and kept only the hard cases.
At Sinai Moses carried God's words to the people and theirs back to God; he wrote the words, read "the book of the covenant", and sprinkled "the blood of the covenant".
Coming down with the tablets, Moses broke them, destroyed the calf, called "Who is on the LORD's side?", and then pleaded for the people: "blot me ... out of thy book".
The tabernacle was set up on the first day of the second year, and the glory of the LORD filled it.
In the second year Moses and Aaron counted every man of twenty and over able to go to war.
Saying "I am not able to bear all this people alone", Moses gathered seventy elders; the LORD put of the spirit on Moses upon them, and they prophesied.

events.label: The spies and the forty years

claim.text: When the people refused to enter the land and spoke of choosing a captain back to Egypt, God sentenced that generation to forty years in the wilderness, all but Caleb and Joshua.
Against Moses' warning the people went up anyway; the Amalekites and Canaanites drove them back to Hormah.
Korah, Dathan and Abiram challenged Moses and Aaron: "Ye take too much upon you"; the ground opened and swallowed them.
Moses struck the rock twice and was told he would not bring the people into the land.
Aaron died on mount Hor in the fortieth year, and his garments passed to Eleazar.
When king Arad attacked, Israel vowed to destroy his cities and did so; the place was called Hormah.
Sihon refused passage and fought at Jahaz; Israel took his land from the Arnon to the Jabbok.
Og fought Israel at Edrei and was defeated, with his sons and people.
Moses sent a thousand from each tribe, with Phinehas, against Midian; five kings of Midian and Balaam were killed.

events.label: Land east of the Jordan given

claim.text: Moses gave the kingdoms of Sihon and Og to Gad, Reuben and half of Manasseh.
Moses asked God to set a man over the congregation; he laid his hands on Joshua before Eleazar and all the people.
In the fortieth year, after Sihon and Og, Moses began to declare the law beyond the Jordan.

events.label: The law written and handed over

claim.text: Moses wrote the law, gave it to the priests and elders, and had the Levites put the book beside the ark.
Before all Israel Moses told Joshua: "Be strong and of a good courage"; God gave Joshua the same charge at the tabernacle.
Moses went up Nebo to the top of Pisgah, saw the land, and died in Moab.

worship.text: The people answered "All the words which the LORD hath said will we do", and the covenant was sealed with blood.
They made a molten calf while Moses was on the mountain; about three thousand died that day.

building.text: Moses "finished the work" of the tabernacle, and the glory of the LORD filled it.

alliances.text: Moses asked Hobab the Midianite to stay as a guide: "thou mayest be to us instead of eyes".
Israel asked Sihon for passage along the king's highway; he refused and fought.

people.text: Rulers of thousands, hundreds, fifties and tens judged the small matters; the hard cases came to Moses.
A second census in the plains of Moab found none of the first generation alive except Caleb and Joshua.
The people often turned against Moses and Aaron: "Would God that we had died in the land of Egypt!"

claim.text: God made Aaron Moses' spokesman before the people and Pharaoh.

quote.text: See, I have made thee a god to Pharaoh: and Aaron thy brother shall be thy prophet.

claim.text: Miriam "the prophetess" led the women after the crossing of the sea; Micah names her with Moses and Aaron as sent before the people.
Two of the seventy prophesied in the camp; when Joshua said "forbid them", Moses answered "would God that all the LORD's people were prophets".
Moses was sent to Pharaoh to bring Israel out of Egypt.
Amalek fought Israel at Rephidim; the LORD swore war with Amalek "from generation to generation".
Edom and Moab refused Israel passage, as Jephthah later recalled; he also asked of Balak king of Moab, "did he ever fight against them".
Both kings were defeated, and their lands given to the tribes east of the Jordan.

rulers.name: Hur, one of five kings of Midian

claim.text: Five kings of Midian, Evi, Rekem, Zur, Hur and Reba, were killed in the war of Numbers 31.

outside.name: Manetho, as quoted by Josephus
outside.date: Quoted by Josephus, late 1st century AD; Manetho was an Egyptian priest-historian

claim.text: Josephus quotes the Egyptian writer Manetho as reporting that the lawgiver of a band of outcasts was a priest of Heliopolis named Osarsiph, who "was called Moses". Josephus rejects the story as fable. It is a hostile Egyptian tradition known only through Josephus, not a record from Moses' time.

twoAccounts.topic: How the judges under Moses were appointed

first.text: Exodus: Jethro sees Moses judging alone and advises him; Moses chooses able men and sets them over thousands, hundreds, fifties and tens.

second.text: Deuteronomy: Moses tells the people "Take you wise men"; they agree, and he makes them heads. Jethro is not named.

questions.question: Are Jethro's judges (Exodus 18), the seventy elders (Numbers 11) and Moses' account in Deuteronomy 1 one event or more than one?

views.label: Two different bodies; Deuteronomy 1 retells Exodus 18

argument.text: Keil reads Deuteronomy 1:12–18 as Moses' own account of the Exodus 18 appointment, and the seventy elders as a separate council given the Spirit to help Moses govern.

views.label: One institution told in different sources
views.holders: Knobel and the critics from Vater onward, as reported by Keil

argument.text: These critics identified the seventy elders with the judges of Exodus 18 and took Deuteronomy 1:9–18 to refer to both, using the differences as evidence of separate documents. Keil reports and rejects this.

questions.question: Who "was king in Jeshurun" in Deuteronomy 33:5: Moses or the LORD?

argument.text: Henry takes the verse "rather" of Moses, who ruled the people after giving them the law, while noting that "some understand this of God himself".
Keil holds that "the subject in ver. 5 is not Moses but Jehovah", who became King in Israel at Sinai.

questions.question: Were the seventy elders the beginning of the later Sanhedrin?

views.label: Yes, a lasting council
views.holders: Talmudists, rabbis and many earlier theologians, as reported by Keil

argument.text: Keil reports the older view that the seventy formed a permanent body that lasted to the Captivity and was revived as the Sanhedrin.

views.label: No, a body for Moses' own time

argument.text: Keil holds that nothing more is recorded of the seventy, and that they did not form a permanent body.

questions.question: When was the Exodus?

views.label: About the middle of the 15th century BC
views.holders: Edward Mack in the ISBE (1915), counting back by 1 Kings 6:1

argument.text: Mack counts the 480 years of 1 Kings 6:1 back from Solomon's temple and reaches "approximately 1448 BC", in Egypt's 18th dynasty.

views.label: In the 13th century BC, under Merenptah

argument.text: Driver argues from Exodus 1:11 that the oppression fell under Rameses II, who built Raamses and Pithom, so the Exodus came under his successor Merenptah.

notSaid: Scripture gives no year BC for Moses or the Exodus, and never names the Pharaoh he faced.

Scripture gives Moses no fixed title for his office. It calls him "the servant of the LORD" and a prophet, and Stephen calls him "a ruler and a deliverer" (Deuteronomy 34:5, 34:10; Acts 7:35). Whether Deuteronomy 33:5 calls him king is disputed.
Moses' sons held no office of rule. They "were named of the tribe of Levi" (1 Chronicles 23:14-15), and the leadership passed to Joshua of Ephraim.
Nothing more is recorded of the seventy elders after Numbers 11.

places.name: Mount Nebo and Pisgah, where he died

rulers.name: Joshua
rulers.title: Leader of Israel after Moses
rulers.tagline: Led Israel over the Jordan and divided the land by lot.

capital.name: Gilgal, the first camp; later Shiloh
capital.note: The tabernacle was set up at Shiloh, where the land was divided.

identifications.text: Moses renamed "Oshea the son of Nun" of Ephraim "Jehoshua".
Chronicles lists "Jehoshua" son of Non in Ephraim's line, and Nehemiah calls him "Jeshua the son of Nun".
The site's person record also attaches Acts 7:45 and Hebrews 4:8 to him: in both verses the KJV's "Jesus" is the Greek form of Joshua's name, and the context is Israel's entry into the land.

burial.text: And they buried him in the border of his inheritance in Timnath-serah, which is in mount Ephraim, on the north side of the hill of Gaash.

reign.text: Not given in Scripture: from Moses' death to his own death at 110

dates.label: Scripture's own numbers
dates.note: Scripture gives no length for Joshua's leadership and no year BC. Caleb's ages imply about seven years of war before the land was divided (see the open question).

dates.label: Josephus: commander for 25 years
dates.note: Josephus, retelling Scripture, gives Joshua 25 years as commander after Moses' death. This is not a BC date.

verdictNotes.text: With the Gibeonites he made a league without asking the LORD: the men "asked not counsel at the mouth of the LORD".

scriptureSays.text: "A man in whom is the spirit"; "full of the spirit of wisdom; for Moses had laid his hands upon him".
God promised him: "as I was with Moses, so I will be with thee".
The LORD "magnified Joshua in the sight of all Israel; and they feared him, as they feared Moses".
"So the LORD was with Joshua; and his fame was noised throughout all the country."
"Israel served the LORD all the days of Joshua", and of the elders who outlived him.
"The servant of the LORD" is the title given him at his death.

accession.text: His first command: Moses sent him to fight Amalek at Rephidim.
He was Moses' "minister", went up the mount with him, and "departed not out of the tabernacle".
One of the twelve spies, he and Caleb urged the people to enter the land, and alone of their generation were promised it.
At Moses' request God named Joshua; Moses laid hands on him before Eleazar and the congregation.
Moses charged him before all Israel, and God charged him at the tabernacle.
After Moses died, the LORD spoke to Joshua; the people answered "All that thou commandest us we will do".

claim.text: Joshua told the officers to prepare: within three days they would cross the Jordan.
From Shittim he sent two spies; Rahab hid them, and they reported that the land's people were afraid.
Israel crossed the Jordan and camped at Gilgal on the tenth day of the first month; that day the LORD "magnified Joshua".
Joshua circumcised the new generation, Israel kept the Passover, and the manna ceased.

events.label: The captain of the LORD's host

claim.text: By Jericho a man with a drawn sword met Joshua as "captain of the host of the LORD"; Joshua bowed and took off his shoes.
Jericho's wall fell; the city was destroyed, and Joshua laid a curse on anyone who rebuilt it.

events.label: Achan and the defeat at Ai

claim.text: Achan took from the devoted spoil; Israel fled before Ai, and Achan was stoned in the valley of Achor.
At God's word Joshua took Ai, burned it and hanged its king.
Joshua built an altar on mount Ebal, wrote a copy of the law on stones, and read all of it to the whole assembly.
Joshua made peace with the Gibeonites; when the trick was found, he kept the oath and made them hewers of wood and drawers of water.
Five Amorite kings attacked Gibeon; Joshua marched all night from Gilgal and routed them; hailstones fell, and "the sun stood still" (quoted from the book of Jasher).
The five kings were taken at Makkedah and put to death; Joshua took the south "at one time" and returned to Gilgal.
Jabin of Hazor gathered the north; Joshua surprised them at the waters of Merom, then took and burned Hazor.
"Joshua made war a long time with all those kings"; only Gibeon made peace; at last "the land rested from war".
The list of kings defeated west of the Jordan ends: "all the kings thirty and one".
When Joshua was old, God told him to divide the land; Eleazar, Joshua and the heads of the tribes gave it out by lot.
Caleb, now 85, asked for the mountain promised at Kadesh; Joshua blessed him and gave him Hebron.
The tabernacle was set up at Shiloh; seven tribes still without land had it surveyed, and Joshua cast lots for them "before the LORD".
Last of all Israel gave Joshua Timnath-serah, which he asked for; he built the city and lived there.

events.label: Cities of refuge and of the Levites

claim.text: Cities of refuge were set apart, and the Levites received their cities, as commanded through Moses.
Joshua blessed Reuben, Gad and half Manasseh and sent them back over the Jordan.
Old, Joshua gathered the leaders, then all the tribes at Shechem: "as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD"; he made a covenant and set up a stone as witness.
Joshua died at 110 and was buried at Timnath-serah.

worship.text: The new generation was circumcised and kept the Passover at Gilgal.
The covenant was renewed at Ebal and again at Shechem.
"Israel served the LORD all the days of Joshua."

building.text: An altar of whole stones on mount Ebal, with the law written on stones.
Joshua built Timnath-serah and lived there.

alliances.text: The one treaty was with Gibeon, sworn by the princes of the congregation.

people.text: The tribes received their land by lot, the Levites cities among them.
Joshua addressed the elders, heads, judges and officers of Israel.
The Gibeonites became hewers of wood and drawers of water for the altar.

claim.text: Five Amorite kings joined against Gibeon for making peace with Israel.
Jabin of Hazor called the northern kings together at the waters of Merom; "Hazor beforetime was the head of all those kingdoms".
The land left to take included "five lords of the Philistines".

first.text: Joshua: "in Timnath-serah, which is in mount Ephraim, on the north side of the hill of Gaash".

second.text: Judges: "in Timnath-heres, in the mount of Ephraim, on the north side of the hill Gaash".

first.text: Joshua 10: Joshua and all Israel took Hebron and Debir and destroyed them.

second.text: Joshua 15 and Judges 1: Caleb (or Judah) drove the sons of Anak from Hebron, and Othniel took Debir for Achsah.

twoAccounts.topic: How much of the land was taken

first.text: "So Joshua took the whole land ... And the land rested from war."

second.text: "Thou art old and stricken in years, and there remaineth yet very much land to be possessed."

questions.question: Timnath-serah or Timnath-heres?

views.label: One place; "heres" (sun) and "serah" are the same letters reversed
views.holders: Moore (1895); Keil treats them as one place (1872 printing)

argument.text: Moore calls "Timnath-heres" in Judges 2:9 "probably a metathesis" of Timnath-serah, made "to get rid of a name of heathenish sound"; Keil simply notes that Timnath-serah is "called Timnath-heres in Judg. ii. 9" and places it at Tibneh.

views.label: Two names, an older and a newer

argument.text: Hävernick took Timnath-heres for the old Canaanite name and Timnath-serah for the Israelite one.

questions.question: Did Joshua take Hebron and Debir, or did Caleb and Othniel?

views.label: Both: the Canaanites came back after Joshua's raid

argument.text: Keil holds that Joshua's campaign did not prevent the Anakim and Canaanites from returning while the army was in the north, so the tribes had to take the towns again when they settled.
Knobel saw a discrepancy between Joshua 10–11 and the Caleb story; Keil reports this view in order to reject it.

questions.question: How long did Joshua lead Israel?

views.label: About seven years of war before the division
views.holders: From the text; Keil's table (1872 printing) also allows seven years

argument.text: Caleb was 40 when sent from Kadesh-barnea and 85 when Hebron was given, "these forty and five years"; the wandering from Kadesh to the brook Zered took 38 years, which leaves about seven years from the crossing to the division.
Josephus gives Joshua 25 years as commander after Moses' death.
Moore notes that Eusebius gives Joshua 27 years.

notSaid: Scripture gives no length for Joshua's leadership and no year BC for the conquest.
Joshua named no successor. After him came "the elders that outlived Joshua" (Judges 2:7), and then the judges.
No prophet is named speaking to Joshua; the LORD speaks to him directly (Joshua 1:1).
Joshua is never called a king or a judge.

places.name: Shittim, the last camp east of the Jordan
Shiloh, where the land was divided

rulers.name: Othniel
rulers.title: Judge of Israel
rulers.tagline: The first judge: eight years under Cushan-rishathaim, then forty years of rest.

identifications.text: The site's family data, from STEP Bible, makes Kenaz Othniel's father and Caleb his uncle. The verses can be read either way (see the open question).

death.text: "And Othniel the son of Kenaz died", after the forty years of rest.

reign.text: "The land had rest forty years"; then Othniel died

dates.label: Scripture's own numbers
dates.note: Eight years of oppression and forty of rest (Judges 3:8, 3:11). No year BC is given; see the group's note on the judges' chronology.

scriptureSays.text: He took Kirjath-sepher (Debir) and received Caleb's daughter Achsah as his wife.
"The LORD raised up a deliverer to the children of Israel, who delivered them, even Othniel the son of Kenaz, Caleb's younger brother."
"The Spirit of the LORD came upon him, and he judged Israel, and went out to war."
In David's time the captain for the twelfth month was "Heldai the Netophathite, of Othniel".

sin.text: Israel "did evil in the sight of the LORD, and forgat the LORD their God, and served Baalim and the groves".

claim.text: The LORD sold them into his hand, and they served him eight years.

cry.text: "The children of Israel cried unto the LORD."

deliverance.text: Othniel went out to war and "his hand prevailed against Chushan-rishathaim".

claim.text: Othniel took Kirjath-sepher, which Caleb had promised to reward with his daughter.
Achsah asked her father for springs of water, and Caleb gave her the upper and nether springs.

events.label: The Spirit comes; war with Chushan-rishathaim

claim.text: The Spirit of the LORD came upon him; he judged Israel and defeated the king of Mesopotamia.
The land had rest forty years, and Othniel died.

worship.text: Israel served Baalim and the groves.

people.text: Israel lived among the Canaanites, Hittites, Amorites, Perizzites, Hivites and Jebusites, intermarried with them, "and served their gods".

claim.text: The first oppressor named in Judges is "Chushan-rishathaim king of Mesopotamia".
Josephus, retelling Judges, calls the oppressors Assyrians, says Othniel drove them back over the Euphrates, and says he "ruled over them forty years" before he died.

first.text: Joshua places the capture during the division of the land under Joshua.

second.text: Judges tells the same capture among the tribes' battles "after the death of Joshua".

questions.question: Was Othniel Caleb's younger brother or his nephew?

views.label: His younger brother
views.holders: Origen, Theodoret, Rashi and others, as listed by Moore; Keil (1865); Moore (1895)

argument.text: Judges 1:13 and 3:9 call Othniel "Caleb's younger brother"; Keil reads the Hebrew accents this way, and Moore says the words "who was younger than he" favour it.

views.label: His nephew, the son of Caleb's brother Kenaz
views.holders: The Greek (LXX, Codex Vaticanus), Calvin, Ewald, Reuss and others, as listed by Moore

argument.text: "The son of Kenaz, the brother of Caleb" (Joshua 15:17) can make Kenaz the brother; 1 Chronicles 4:13 counts Othniel among "the sons of Kenaz".

questions.question: How long was the time of the judges, and how do Scripture's numbers fit together?

views.label: One after another, a long period
views.holders: Josephus (about AD 93); the earlier chronologists who matched the sum to Acts 13:20, as reported by Keil

argument.text: Josephus counts 592 years from the Exodus to the temple, a figure Keil shows can be reached by adding Judges' numbers in sequence; earlier chronologists also read the KJV's "four hundred and fifty years" in Acts 13:20 as the judges' total.

views.label: Some periods overlap
views.holders: Sebastian Schmid (1684), Keil (1865), Ewald and Hengstenberg, as listed by Moore; Mack in the ISBE (1915)

argument.text: Judges 10:7 sells Israel to the Philistines and the Ammonites together, so the two oppressions can run at the same time; Samson judged "in the days of the Philistines". On Keil's reckoning the totals then fit 1 Kings 6:1. Mack also makes Ibzan, Elon and Abdon partly overlap Jephthah and Samson.
Moore notes how often 40, 80 and 20 recur and reads 1 Kings 6:1's 480 years as twelve generations of forty, a systematic chronology in which years of foreign rule are not counted.

views.label: A much shorter period
views.holders: Lepsius and Bunsen, as reported by Keil

argument.text: Starting from the view that the numbers are round, Lepsius and Bunsen held that the whole period lasted only 169 to 187 years. Keil reports this in order to reject it.

notSaid: Scripture gives no year BC for Othniel and says nothing of his rule beyond the war and the forty years of rest.
Judges 3 does not name his tribe; his family belongs to Caleb, who received land "among the children of Judah" (Joshua 15:13).

rulers.name: Ehud
rulers.title: Judge of Israel
rulers.tagline: Struck down Eglon of Moab; the land had rest eighty years.

identifications.text: The site's family data, from STEP Bible, links "Gera" to the son of Benjamin in Genesis 46:21 and attaches the "sons of Ehud" of 1 Chronicles 8:6 to this Ehud. Judges states neither link.

reign.text: Not given; after the victory "the land had rest fourscore years"

dates.label: Scripture's own numbers
dates.note: Eighteen years of oppression and eighty of rest (Judges 3:14, 3:30). No year BC is given.

scriptureSays.text: "The LORD raised them up a deliverer, Ehud the son of Gera, a Benjamite, a man lefthanded."
To Eglon he said: "I have a message from God unto thee."
To Israel: "Follow after me: for the LORD hath delivered your enemies the Moabites into your hand."
"So Moab was subdued that day under the hand of Israel."

sin.text: "The children of Israel did evil again in the sight of the LORD."

claim.text: With Ammon and Amalek, Eglon took "the city of palm trees", and Israel served him eighteen years.

cry.text: "When the children of Israel cried unto the LORD, the LORD raised them up a deliverer."

deliverance.text: Ehud killed Eglon, then led Israel down from mount Ephraim, held the fords of the Jordan and killed about ten thousand Moabites.

claim.text: Israel sent tribute to Eglon by Ehud, who had made a two-edged dagger and hidden it on his right thigh.
Alone with the king in his summer parlour, Ehud drove the dagger into him and locked the doors behind him.
Ehud escaped to Seirath and blew a trumpet in mount Ephraim.
Israel held the fords toward Moab and killed about ten thousand men; "there escaped not a man".
"The land had rest fourscore years."
Eglon gathered the children of Ammon and Amalek and took the city of palm trees.
Josephus, retelling Judges, says Ehud "held the government eighty years" and that Shamgar, elected after him, died in his first year. Neither detail is in Judges.

views.label: Some periods overlap
views.holders: Sebastian Schmid (1684), Keil (1865), Ewald and Hengstenberg, as listed by Moore; Mack in the ISBE (1915)

notSaid: Judges calls Ehud a "deliverer" (3:15) but never says that he "judged Israel".
Scripture does not say what Ehud did during the eighty years of rest; the next notice is "when Ehud was dead" (Judges 4:1).
Shamgar, who "also delivered Israel" with an ox goad after Ehud (Judges 3:31), is not given a page here: the text never says he judged.

rulers.name: Deborah
rulers.title: Prophetess and judge
rulers.tagline: Judged Israel under her palm tree; with Barak she broke Jabin of Hazor.
rulers.tribe: Not stated (she lived in mount Ephraim)

identifications.text: "Deborah, a prophetess, the wife of Lapidoth, she judged Israel at that time."

reign.text: The years of her judging are not given; after the victory "the land had rest forty years"

dates.label: Scripture's own numbers
dates.note: Twenty years of oppression, then forty of rest (Judges 4:3, 5:31). No year BC is given.

scriptureSays.text: "She dwelt under the palm tree of Deborah between Ramah and Beth-el in mount Ephraim: and the children of Israel came up to her for judgment."
She called Barak and gave him the LORD's command to go to mount Tabor; when he would not go without her, she went, saying the LORD would "sell Sisera into the hand of a woman".
"Up; for this is the day in which the LORD hath delivered Sisera into thine hand."
In the song: "until that I Deborah arose, that I arose a mother in Israel".

sin.text: "The children of Israel again did evil in the sight of the LORD, when Ehud was dead."

oppressor.name: Jabin, king of Canaan, who reigned in Hazor

claim.text: Jabin's captain Sisera had nine hundred chariots of iron, and "twenty years he mightily oppressed the children of Israel".

cry.text: "The children of Israel cried unto the LORD."

deliverance.text: The LORD routed Sisera before Barak at the Kishon; Jael killed Sisera; Israel prevailed until Jabin was destroyed.

claim.text: Israel came to Deborah for judgment between Ramah and Beth-el.
Deborah sent for Barak of Kedesh-naphtali with the LORD's command to take ten thousand men of Naphtali and Zebulun to mount Tabor.
Barak called Zebulun and Naphtali to Kedesh, and Deborah went up with him.
Barak came down from Tabor; the LORD routed Sisera's chariots and army, and Barak pursued them to Harosheth.
Sisera fled on foot to the tent of Jael, wife of Heber the Kenite, who killed him with a tent nail.
Israel's hand "prevailed against Jabin the king of Canaan, until they had destroyed Jabin".

events.label: The song of Deborah and Barak

claim.text: Deborah and Barak sang of the victory, praising the tribes that came and rebuking those that stayed away.
"And the land had rest forty years."

worship.text: "They chose new gods; then was war in the gates."

alliances.text: Heber the Kenite had separated from his people, and "there was peace between Jabin the king of Hazor and the house of Heber".

people.text: Before Deborah arose, "the highways were unoccupied" and village life had ceased.
Ephraim, Benjamin, Machir, Zebulun, Issachar and Naphtali came; Reuben, Gilead, Dan and Asher stayed away; Meroz was cursed for not helping.

claim.text: As prophetess she gave Barak the LORD's command and the day of battle.

quote.text: Hath not the LORD God of Israel commanded, saying, Go and draw toward mount Tabor, and take with thee ten thousand men of the children of Naphtali and of the children of Zebulun?

rulers.name: Jabin, king of Canaan in Hazor

claim.text: "The kings of Canaan" fought "in Taanach by the waters of Megiddo".

first.text: Prose (Judges 4): Barak takes ten thousand men of Naphtali and Zebulun.

second.text: Song (Judges 5): Ephraim, Benjamin, Machir, Zebulun, Issachar and Naphtali are praised.

first.text: Prose: Jael drove a tent nail into his temples while "he was fast asleep and weary".

second.text: Song: she gave him milk, struck him with the hammer, and "at her feet he bowed, he fell".

questions.question: Do Judges 4 and Judges 5 tell the battle differently?

views.label: The song is a poetic retelling of the same events

argument.text: Keil reads the song's words as heaping up verbs "for the purpose of depicting the boldness and greatness of the deed", not as a second version of how Sisera died.

views.label: Two different versions, the song the older

argument.text: Moore lists three differences: Sisera as a king or as Jabin's general, the whole people or two tribes in the battle, and the manner of Sisera's death; he holds the song to be older than the prose.

questions.question: Where was Deborah from?

argument.text: Judges 4:5 places her seat "between Ramah and Beth-el in mount Ephraim".

views.label: Issachar, near the plain of Jezreel

argument.text: Moore suggests that "the princes of Issachar were with Deborah" (5:15) points to Issachar, perhaps Daberath, and that the palm tree's name drew her to Ephraim.

questions.question: Who is "Bedan" among the deliverers Samuel names in 1 Samuel 12:11?

views.label: Barak
views.holders: The Greek (LXX), Syriac and Arabic versions; Keil (1866); Thenius, Wellhausen and Driver, as listed by Moore

argument.text: No judge called Bedan appears in Judges; reading Barak puts the celebrated victor of Judges 4 beside Gideon and Jephthah, as in Hebrews 11:32. The site's person data follows this view and attaches the verse to Barak.
Ewald proposed restoring Abdon for Bedan.

views.label: Jair
views.holders: Some commentators, as reported by Keil

argument.text: Because a Bedan appears in Manasseh's line in Gilead (1 Chronicles 7:17), some took him for Jair the Gileadite; Keil calls this arbitrary.
Kimchi read Bedan as "ben-Dan", the Danite, meaning Samson.

notSaid: Scripture does not name Deborah's tribe, give the years she judged, or record her death.
Hebrews 11:32 names Barak, not Deborah; 1 Samuel 12:11 names "Bedan" (see the open question).
Barak is never said to judge; he commands the army under her word (Judges 4:6-10). He has no page of his own here.
"Harosheth of the Gentiles", Sisera's city, is not yet in the site's atlas.

places.name: The palm tree between Ramah and Beth-el

rulers.name: Gideon
rulers.title: Judge of Israel
rulers.tagline: Three hundred men against Midian; forty years of quiet; he refused the crown.

identifications.text: After he threw down Baal's altar his father called him Jerubbaal; "Jerubbaal, who is Gideon".
The site's person record also attaches 2 Samuel 11:21, which names "Abimelech the son of Jerubbesheth": the same man, with the name formed differently.

death.text: "Gideon the son of Joash died in a good old age."

burial.text: was buried in the sepulchre of Joash his father, in Ophrah of the Abi-ezrites

reign.text: Not given as years of judging; "the country was in quietness forty years in the days of Gideon"

dates.label: Scripture's own numbers
dates.note: Seven years under Midian, then forty years of quiet (Judges 6:1, 8:28). No year BC is given.

verdictNotes.text: From the Midianite gold he made an ephod at Ophrah: "all Israel went thither a whoring after it: which thing became a snare unto Gideon, and to his house."
After his death Israel made Baal-berith their god and showed no kindness to his house.

scriptureSays.text: The angel of the LORD greeted him: "The LORD is with thee, thou mighty man of valour."
Gideon answered: "my family is poor in Manasseh, and I am the least in my father's house."
"The Spirit of the LORD came upon Gideon, and he blew a trumpet."
Offered a dynasty, he said: "I will not rule over you, neither shall my son rule over you: the LORD shall rule over you."
Later Scripture remembers "the day of Midian" and "the slaughter of Midian at the rock of Oreb".
Samuel names Jerubbaal among Israel's deliverers, and Hebrews among those who acted by faith.

sin.text: "The children of Israel did evil in the sight of the LORD."

oppressor.name: Midian, with the Amalekites and "the children of the east"

claim.text: For seven years they came up at harvest "as grasshoppers for multitude", and Israel hid in dens and caves.

cry.text: "Israel was greatly impoverished because of the Midianites; and the children of Israel cried unto the LORD."

deliverance.text: With three hundred men, trumpets and lamps in pitchers, Gideon routed Midian; he then captured its kings beyond the Jordan.

accession.text: The angel of the LORD found him threshing wheat in a winepress at Ophrah to hide it from Midian, and sent him: "have not I sent thee?"
Fire from the rock consumed his offering; he built the altar "Jehovah-shalom".
By night he threw down his father's altar of Baal and cut down the grove.
He asked for the sign of the fleece, wet and then dry.

claim.text: Gideon destroyed his father's altar of Baal; Joash told the men of the city "if he be a god, let him plead for himself".
Abi-ezer, Manasseh, Asher, Zebulun and Naphtali answered his trumpet.
The fearful went home; at the water three hundred who lapped were kept: "lest Israel vaunt themselves against me".

events.label: The dream of the barley cake

claim.text: In the Midianite camp Gideon heard a dream read as "the sword of Gideon", and worshipped.
Three companies broke their pitchers and cried "The sword of the LORD, and of Gideon"; the host turned on itself and fled.
Ephraim held the waters and killed the princes Oreb and Zeeb.
Ephraim complained they were not called; Gideon answered "Is not the gleaning of the grapes of Ephraim better than the vintage of Abi-ezer?"
The men of Succoth and Penuel would not feed his faint army.
At Karkor Gideon struck the host and took Zebah and Zalmunna.
He "taught the men of Succoth" with thorns and briers, broke down Penuel's tower and killed its men.
Learning they had killed his brothers at Tabor, Gideon killed the two kings.
"The LORD shall rule over you."
He made an ephod of the gold and put it in Ophrah; it became a snare.
The country was quiet forty years; Gideon died old and was buried at Ophrah.

worship.text: A prophet reminded Israel of the Exodus: "ye have not obeyed my voice".
The altar of Baal at Ophrah was destroyed, and an altar to the LORD built in its place.
Gideon's ephod became an object Israel "went a whoring after"; after his death they made Baal-berith their god.

building.text: Gideon built the altar "Jehovah-shalom" at Ophrah.

alliances.text: He called Asher, Zebulun, Naphtali and later Ephraim to the war.

people.text: Israel hid in "dens which are in the mountains, and caves, and strong holds".
The men of Israel offered: "Rule thou over us, both thou, and thy son, and thy son's son also."
Gideon had seventy sons and many wives; his son Abimelech by a concubine in Shechem later made himself king.

claim.text: When Israel cried to the LORD, he sent a prophet who recalled the Exodus and rebuked their worship of the Amorites' gods.

quote.text: I am the LORD your God; fear not the gods of the Amorites, in whose land ye dwell: but ye have not obeyed my voice.

worldStage.power: Midian, with Amalek and "the children of the east"

claim.text: Their camels were "without number, as the sand by the sea side"; a hundred and twenty thousand of them fell.

questions.question: What was Gideon's ephod?

views.label: A priestly garment used to ask the LORD's will

argument.text: Keil holds that "ephod" means the high priest's shoulder-dress with its breastplate, and that Gideon probably wore it to seek revelations; the sin lay in setting up worship outside the sanctuary.

views.label: An image or idol
views.holders: Gesenius and others, as reported by Keil; Moore (1895); Bertheau held it was a golden bull image of the LORD, as reported by Keil

argument.text: Moore takes "ephod" here as "the specific name of a kind of idol", pointing to the weight of gold and to the editor's phrase "went a whoring after it".

questions.question: How long was the time of the judges, and how do Scripture's numbers fit together?

views.label: One after another, a long period
views.holders: Josephus (about AD 93); the earlier chronologists who matched the sum to Acts 13:20, as reported by Keil

argument.text: Josephus counts 592 years from the Exodus to the temple, a figure Keil shows can be reached by adding Judges' numbers in sequence; earlier chronologists also read the KJV's "four hundred and fifty years" in Acts 13:20 as the judges' total.

views.label: Some periods overlap
views.holders: Sebastian Schmid (1684), Keil (1865), Ewald and Hengstenberg, as listed by Moore; Mack in the ISBE (1915)

argument.text: Judges 10:7 sells Israel to the Philistines and the Ammonites together, so the two oppressions can run at the same time; Samson judged "in the days of the Philistines". Moore notes how often 40, 80 and 20 recur and reads 1 Kings 6:1's 480 years as twelve generations of forty, a systematic chronology in which years of foreign rule are not counted.

views.label: A much shorter period
views.holders: Lepsius and Bunsen, as reported by Keil

argument.text: Starting from the view that the numbers are round, Lepsius and Bunsen held that the whole period lasted only 169 to 187 years. Keil reports this in order to reject it.

notSaid: Judges never says that Gideon "judged Israel"; it says the country was quiet forty years "in the days of Gideon" (Judges 8:28).
Scripture does not say what the ephod looked like or how it was used (see the open question).
Abimelech, Gideon's son, "reigned three years over Israel" from Shechem (Judges 9:22) but is not called a judge; he has no page here.

rulers.name: Tola
rulers.title: Judge of Israel
rulers.tagline: Rose "to defend Israel" after Abimelech; judged twenty-three years from Shamir.

identifications.text: "Tola" and "Puah" (Phuvah) are also the names of two of Issachar's sons; Moore takes this as a sign that the names are those of clans.

death.text: Tola judged Israel twenty-three years and died.

dates.label: Scripture's own numbers
dates.note: 23 years of judging (Judges 10:2). No year BC is given.

scriptureSays.text: He was "a man of Issachar" who "dwelt in Shamir in mount Ephraim".
"He judged Israel twenty and three years, and died."

deliverance.text: "After Abimelech there arose to defend Israel Tola the son of Puah, the son of Dodo, a man of Issachar."

claim.text: "After Abimelech there arose to defend Israel Tola the son of Puah, the son of Dodo, a man of Issachar."
Tola judged Israel twenty-three years and died.
Josephus's retelling of Judges passes from Abimelech straight to Jair and leaves Tola out.

Tola's predecessor in the text is Abimelech, Gideon's son, who made himself king (Judges 10:1); Abimelech is not counted as a judge on these pages.

rulers.name: Jair
rulers.title: Judge of Israel
rulers.tagline: A Gileadite who judged twenty-two years; thirty sons on thirty ass colts.

identifications.text: The site keeps the judge separate from "Jair the son of Manasseh" of Moses' time (jair-num-32-41), who also named towns Havoth-jair.

burial.text: And Jair died, and was buried in Camon.

dates.label: Scripture's own numbers
dates.note: 22 years of judging (Judges 10:3). No year BC is given.

scriptureSays.text: "He had thirty sons that rode on thirty ass colts, and they had thirty cities, which are called Havoth-jair unto this day."

deliverance.text: "After him arose Jair, a Gileadite, and judged Israel twenty and two years."

claim.text: "After him arose Jair, a Gileadite, and judged Israel twenty and two years."
Jair died after twenty-two years.

people.text: His thirty sons rode thirty ass colts and held thirty cities in Gilead.

first.text: Numbers and Deuteronomy: Jair the son of Manasseh took the towns in Moses' time and called them after himself.

second.text: Judges: the judge's thirty sons had thirty cities "which are called Havoth-jair unto this day".

views.label: An old name brought back into use

argument.text: Keil holds that Judges does not say the towns were first named by the judge, only that the old name was used again for his sons' cities.

views.label: One clan tradition told in two places

argument.text: Moore reads Numbers 32:41 and Judges 10:4 as agreeing notices about the clan of Jair in Gilead, and the passages that put the towns in Bashan as later misunderstanding.

Judges does not name Jair's tribe; Gilead lay east of the Jordan.

rulers.name: Jephthah
rulers.title: Judge of Israel
rulers.tagline: Chosen head of Gilead; broke Ammon; judged Israel six years.

identifications.text: "Jephthah the Gileadite was a mighty man of valour, and he was the son of an harlot: and Gilead begat Jephthah."

death.text: Jephthah died after judging Israel six years.

burial.text: Then died Jephthah the Gileadite, and was buried in one of the cities of Gilead.

dates.label: Scripture's own numbers
dates.note: Eighteen years of Ammonite oppression and six years of judging (Judges 10:8, 12:7). Jephthah's "three hundred years" (11:26) is Scripture's own long count; see the open question.

scriptureSays.text: "Then the Spirit of the LORD came upon Jephthah."
He laid Israel's case before the king of Ammon: "the LORD the Judge be judge this day between the children of Israel and the children of Ammon".
Samuel names him among the deliverers; Hebrews among those who acted by faith.

sin.text: Israel served Baalim, Ashtaroth and the gods of Syria, Zidon, Moab, Ammon and the Philistines.

claim.text: The LORD sold Israel to the Philistines and the Ammonites; for eighteen years the Ammonites oppressed Israel in Gilead, and crossed the Jordan to fight Judah, Benjamin and Ephraim.

cry.text: Israel cried "We have sinned"; the LORD answered "I will deliver you no more"; they put away the strange gods, and "his soul was grieved for the misery of Israel".

deliverance.text: Jephthah struck Ammon "from Aroer, even till thou come to Minnith, even twenty cities".

accession.text: His half-brothers drove him out; he lived in the land of Tob, where "vain men" gathered to him.
When Ammon made war, the elders of Gilead came to fetch him as captain.
He asked, "shall I be your head?"; the people made him "head and captain over them", and he spoke all his words before the LORD in Mizpeh.

claim.text: At Mizpeh the people made Jephthah head and captain.
Jephthah sent messengers recounting how Israel had taken Sihon's land from the Arnon to the Jabbok, and had held it three hundred years.
Jephthah vowed that whatever came out of his house to meet him should be the LORD's, "and I will offer it up for a burnt offering".
He struck twenty cities from Aroer to Minnith: "the children of Ammon were subdued".
His only child came out to meet him; after two months on the mountains he "did with her according to his vow", and the daughters of Israel lamented her four days a year.
Ephraim threatened to burn his house; Gilead took the fords of the Jordan, and forty-two thousand who said "Sibboleth" fell.
Jephthah judged Israel six years and was buried in a city of Gilead.

worship.text: Israel put away the strange gods "and served the LORD".
"It was a custom in Israel" for the daughters of Israel to lament Jephthah's daughter four days a year.

alliances.text: Jephthah tried words before war, but "the king of the children of Ammon hearkened not".

people.text: The elders of Gilead bound themselves by oath to make him their head.
Gilead and Ephraim fought each other at the fords of the Jordan.

rulers.name: The king of the children of Ammon (not named)

claim.text: The king claimed the land "from Arnon even unto Jabbok" as taken from him at the Exodus.
Israel was sold into the hands of the Philistines as well as Ammon.

questions.question: Did Jephthah offer his daughter as a burnt offering?

views.label: Yes, she was sacrificed
views.holders: Josephus (about AD 93); the older Jewish and Christian interpreters, as listed by Moore; Moore (1895)

argument.text: Josephus says "he sacrificed his daughter as a burnt-offering", an offering "neither conformable to the law nor acceptable to God". Moore reports that early interpreters without exception read the text this way, and holds it himself.

views.label: No, she was given to the LORD in lifelong virginity
views.holders: First found in the Kimchis (late 12th century), as reported by Moore; Keil (1865)

argument.text: Keil reads "she knew no man" as the way the vow was fulfilled, a "spiritual burnt-offering, in a lifelong chastity", and argues that the writer would not have described a human sacrifice without blame.

questions.question: What do Jephthah's "three hundred years" measure?

views.label: From the settling of Gilead to Jephthah, with the judges in sequence

argument.text: Keil counts 301 years in Judges from Cushan-rishathaim to the Ammonite oppression, plus about ten years after the division, and finds that Jephthah could fairly speak of 300 years.

views.label: A round figure reaching to Samson's time too, with overlaps

argument.text: Mack takes the Ammonite and Philistine oppressions as roughly at the same time, so that the 300 years reach from Joshua's entry to the age of Samson as well as of Jephthah.

rulers.name: Ibzan
rulers.title: Judge of Israel
rulers.tagline: Judged seven years from Beth-lehem; thirty sons and thirty daughters.

burial.text: Then died Ibzan, and was buried at Beth-lehem.

dates.label: Scripture's own numbers
dates.note: 7 years of judging (Judges 12:9). No year BC is given.

scriptureSays.text: "He had thirty sons, and thirty daughters, whom he sent abroad, and took in thirty daughters from abroad for his sons."

deliverance.text: "And after him Ibzan of Beth-lehem judged Israel."

claim.text: "And after him Ibzan of Beth-lehem judged Israel."
Ibzan died after seven years.

people.text: He married his thirty daughters outside the family and brought in thirty wives for his sons.

rulers.name: Samson
rulers.title: Judge of Israel
rulers.tagline: A Nazarite who judged Israel twenty years "in the days of the Philistines".

death.text: He pulled down the house of Dagon on the Philistine lords and died with them.

burial.text: buried him between Zorah and Eshtaol in the buryingplace of Manoah his father

reign.text: "He judged Israel in the days of the Philistines twenty years"

dates.label: Scripture's own numbers
dates.note: Twenty years of judging inside, or after, the forty years of Philistine rule (Judges 13:1, 15:20, 16:31); see the open question.

scriptureSays.text: "The child shall be a Nazarite unto God from the womb: and he shall begin to deliver Israel out of the hand of the Philistines."
The Spirit of the LORD came upon him again and again.
His marriage at Timnath "was of the LORD, that he sought an occasion against the Philistines".
When he was shaven, "he wist not that the LORD was departed from him".
"The dead which he slew at his death were more than they which he slew in his life."
Hebrews names him among those who acted by faith.

sin.text: "The children of Israel did evil again in the sight of the LORD."

claim.text: "The LORD delivered them into the hand of the Philistines forty years."

deliverance.text: He was to "begin to deliver Israel"; he fought the Philistines alone, and at his death killed their lords in Dagon's house.

accession.text: The angel of the LORD told Manoah's barren wife she would bear a son who must be a Nazarite.
Manoah offered a kid, and the angel ascended in the flame of the altar.
"The woman bare a son, and called his name Samson"; the Spirit began to move him between Zorah and Eshtaol.

claim.text: Samson chose a Philistine wife at Timnath; on the way he tore a lion apart with his hands.
When his riddle was found out, he killed thirty men at Ashkelon to pay the wager.
His wife given to another, he burned the Philistines' corn, vineyards and olives with three hundred foxes.

events.label: Hip and thigh; the rock Etam

claim.text: After the Philistines burned his wife and her father, he struck them "with a great slaughter" and went to the rock Etam.
Three thousand men of Judah bound him to hand him over: "Knowest thou not that the Philistines are rulers over us?"
The cords melted, and with the jawbone of an ass he killed a thousand men; God gave him water at En-hakkore.
At Gaza he "saw there an harlot, and went in unto her"; the Gazites lay in wait all night, but at midnight he took the doors of the city gate and carried them to a hill before Hebron.
The Philistine lords paid Delilah to learn his secret; she had his seven locks shaved.
The Philistines put out his eyes and set him grinding in the prison house at Gaza.
Brought out for sport at the feast of Dagon, he prayed for strength "only this once" and pulled down the pillars.
His brothers buried him between Zorah and Eshtaol.

worship.text: The Philistines held a great sacrifice to Dagon, saying "Our god hath delivered Samson our enemy into our hand".

alliances.text: "At that time the Philistines had dominion over Israel."

people.text: The men of Judah accepted Philistine rule and handed Samson over.

rulers.name: The lords of the Philistines (not named)

claim.text: Each lord offered Delilah eleven hundred pieces of silver; all of them were in Dagon's house when it fell.

questions.question: Do Samson's twenty years fall inside the Philistines' forty?

argument.text: Keil reads "in the days of the Philistines" as "during the oppression of the Philistines", so Samson's years are not added separately; Moore's scheme also counts the forty as Samson's twenty and Eli's twenty.

views.label: Counted separately
views.holders: The reckoning behind Josephus's 612 years, as worked out by Keil

argument.text: Keil shows that counting Samson's twenty years apart from the Philistines' forty gives 410 years for Judges, which with Josephus's other figures makes his total of 612 years from the Exodus to the temple (Antiquities 20.10); his other total, 592 years (Antiquities 8.3.1), fits 390, with Samson inside the forty.

rulers.name: Eli
rulers.title: Priest and judge of Israel
rulers.tagline: The priest at Shiloh who judged Israel forty years.

identifications.text: Eli's descent from Aaron's son Ithamar is inferred: his great-grandson Ahimelech (1 Samuel 14:3; 22:20) is "of the sons of Ithamar" in 1 Chronicles 24:3. Keil draws this inference.
Josephus, retelling Samuel, says Eli was the first of Ithamar's family to hold the high priesthood, after the line of Eleazar.

death.text: Hearing that the ark was taken, Eli fell backward from his seat by the gate and broke his neck, aged ninety-eight.

reign.text: "He had judged Israel forty years" (the Greek text reads twenty)

dates.label: Scripture's own numbers
dates.note: Forty years in the Hebrew and the KJV (1 Samuel 4:18); the Greek (LXX) reads twenty. No year BC is given.

verdictNotes.text: The man of God said Eli honoured his sons above the LORD, and that his house would lose its old men and its place.
The word was fulfilled when Solomon removed Abiathar from the priesthood.

scriptureSays.text: "Eli the priest sat upon a seat by a post of the temple of the LORD."
He blessed Hannah: "the God of Israel grant thee thy petition".
He heard what his sons did and asked, "Why do ye such things?", but "they hearkened not unto the voice of their father".
God's charge against him: "his sons made themselves vile, and he restrained them not".
His answer to the judgment: "It is the LORD: let him do what seemeth him good."
"His heart trembled for the ark of God."

claim.text: Eli saw Hannah praying at Shiloh, blessed her, and received the child Samuel to minister before the LORD.
Hophni and Phinehas took the offerings by force "for men abhorred the offering of the LORD".

events.label: The warning of the man of God

claim.text: A man of God announced that both sons would die on one day and that God would raise up a faithful priest.
Eli taught the boy to answer "Speak, LORD; for thy servant heareth", and heard from him the judgment on his house.
The Philistines defeated Israel at Ebenezer, took the ark, and killed Hophni and Phinehas.
At the news Eli fell from his seat and died; his daughter-in-law named her son I-chabod, "The glory is departed".

worship.text: Israel went up yearly to sacrifice at Shiloh, where Eli's sons were priests.
"The word of the LORD was precious in those days; there was no open vision."
The elders fetched the ark into battle, hoping "it may save us".

people.text: Israel was beaten twice by the Philistines, losing about four thousand and then thirty thousand men.

claim.text: He brought the judgment on Eli's house.

quote.text: them that honour me I will honour, and they that despise me shall be lightly esteemed

claim.text: The boy Samuel told Eli "every whit" of the LORD's word against his house.

quote.text: Behold, I will do a thing in Israel, at which both the ears of every one that heareth it shall tingle.

claim.text: The Philistines camped at Aphek, defeated Israel and captured the ark.

questions.question: Did Eli judge Israel forty years or twenty?

argument.text: Keil holds that the Greek reading twenty "does not deserve the slightest notice", since Eli would then have become judge at seventy-eight.
Moore adopts the Greek twenty, so that Samson's twenty and Eli's twenty fill the Philistines' forty years.

rulers.name: Samuel
rulers.title: Prophet and last judge of Israel
rulers.tagline: Judged Israel all his life from Ramah, and anointed its first two kings.
rulers.tribe: Levi in 1 Chronicles 6; his father is called an Ephrathite of mount Ephraim (1 Samuel 1:1)

identifications.text: Chronicles places Samuel ("Shemuel") in the Levite line of Kohath, as father of Joel and grandfather of the singer Heman.

death.text: "Samuel died; and all the Israelites were gathered together, and lamented him."

burial.text: buried him in his house at Ramah

reign.text: "Samuel judged Israel all the days of his life"; no number of years is given

dates.label: Scripture's own numbers
dates.note: Scripture gives no length for Samuel's judgeship and no year BC. Twenty years passed between the ark's return and the assembly at Mizpeh (1 Samuel 7:2).

dates.label: Josephus: 12 years alone, 18 with Saul
dates.note: Josephus, retelling Samuel, says Samuel governed alone for twelve years after Eli's death and eighteen years together with Saul. This is not a BC date.

verdictNotes.text: His sons, made judges in Beer-sheba, "walked not in his ways, but turned aside after lucre, and took bribes".

scriptureSays.text: "The LORD was with him, and did let none of his words fall to the ground"; all Israel "knew that Samuel was established to be a prophet of the LORD".
He went yearly in circuit to Beth-el, Gilgal and Mizpeh, and judged Israel at home in Ramah.
At the end, he asked the people to witness against him, and they answered "Thou hast not defrauded us, nor oppressed us".
"God forbid that I should sin against the LORD in ceasing to pray for you."
Later Scripture sets him beside Moses as one who called on the LORD and stood before him.
Peter counts the prophets "from Samuel"; Paul says God gave judges "until Samuel the prophet".
"The acts of David the king ... are written in the book of Samuel the seer."

sin.text: Israel had "strange gods and Ashtaroth" among them; at Samuel's word "the children of Israel did put away Baalim and Ashtaroth, and served the LORD only".

claim.text: The Philistines had taken the ark and Israel's cities; when Israel gathered at Mizpeh, their lords went up against them.

cry.text: Israel fasted and confessed "We have sinned", and begged Samuel "Cease not to cry unto the LORD our God for us".

deliverance.text: As Samuel offered a lamb, "the LORD thundered with a great thunder" on the Philistines; "they came no more into the coast of Israel".

accession.text: Hannah named him Samuel, "Because I have asked him of the LORD", and lent him to the LORD at Shiloh.
"The child did minister unto the LORD before Eli the priest."
The LORD called him by night: "Speak; for thy servant heareth."
"The word of Samuel came to all Israel."

claim.text: Israel put away its idols, poured out water before the LORD and fasted; "Samuel judged the children of Israel in Mizpeh".
The LORD thundered on the Philistines; Samuel set up a stone, "Hitherto hath the LORD helped us".
The cities from Ekron to Gath came back to Israel, "and there was peace between Israel and the Amorites".
Samuel judged at Beth-el, Gilgal and Mizpeh, and built an altar at Ramah.
Old, he made his sons Joel and Abiah judges in Beer-sheba.
The elders asked "make us a king to judge us like all the nations"; God said "they have not rejected thee, but they have rejected me", and Samuel warned them of "the manner of the king".
God told Samuel to anoint a man of Benjamin; Samuel poured oil on Saul's head.
Saul was taken by lot; Samuel wrote "the manner of the kingdom" in a book and laid it up before the LORD.
After the victory over Ammon, all the people made Saul king at Gilgal.
Samuel recounted the LORD's deeds from Moses to the judges, called down thunder and rain at wheat harvest, and promised to keep praying for them.
When Saul offered the burnt offering himself, Samuel told him "thy kingdom shall not continue".
"To obey is better than sacrifice"; Samuel told Saul the LORD had rejected him, hewed Agag in pieces, and "came no more to see Saul until the day of his death".
Sent to Jesse the Beth-lehemite, Samuel anointed David "in the midst of his brethren".
David fled to Samuel at Ramah; Saul's messengers met "the company of the prophets" with Samuel over them, and prophesied.
All Israel lamented Samuel and buried him at Ramah.
When Saul sought him through a woman at Endor, Samuel's words were: "to morrow shalt thou and thy sons be with me".

worship.text: Israel "did put away Baalim and Ashtaroth, and served the LORD only".
No later Passover was like Josiah's "from the days of Samuel the prophet".

building.text: He built an altar to the LORD at Ramah.
He set up the stone Eben-ezer between Mizpeh and Shen.

alliances.text: "There was peace between Israel and the Amorites."

people.text: Samuel wrote "the manner of the kingdom" in a book and laid it up before the LORD.
Chronicles says David and "Samuel the seer" ordained the gatekeepers, and lists things Samuel dedicated.

claim.text: A prophet from his youth, he gave the word of the LORD to Eli, to the people and to Saul.

quote.text: And all Israel from Dan even to Beer-sheba knew that Samuel was established to be a prophet of the LORD.

claim.text: At Naioth Samuel stood "as appointed over them".
Subdued at Ebenezer, "the hand of the LORD was against the Philistines all the days of Samuel".
Samuel says Nahash's attack was the moment Israel demanded a king.
Samuel sent Saul against Amalek and himself put Agag to death.

first.text: 1 Samuel: "the name of his firstborn was Joel; and the name of his second, Abiah".

second.text: 1 Chronicles 6:28: "the firstborn Vashni, and Abiah"; a few verses later Heman is "the son of Joel, the son of Shemuel".

first.text: 1 Samuel: Elkanah of Ramathaim-zophim "of mount Ephraim" was "an Ephrathite".

second.text: 1 Chronicles: Elkanah and Samuel stand in the Levite line of Kohath.

questions.question: Was Samuel's firstborn Joel or Vashni?

views.label: Joel; his name has dropped out of 1 Chronicles 6:28

argument.text: Keil holds that the name of the firstborn, Joel, is missing from the verse, as 1 Chronicles 6:33 and 1 Samuel 8:2 show. The site's person data likewise attaches 1 Chronicles 6:28 to Joel.

views.label: Vashni, as the KJV prints it
views.holders: The KJV translators' reading of the verse

argument.text: The KJV renders the verse as a name, "the firstborn Vashni".

questions.question: Was Samuel a Levite?

views.label: Yes; "Ephrathite" means he lived in Ephraim

argument.text: Keil holds that the Chronicles genealogy shows Samuel's Levite descent, and that "Ephrathite" describes Elkanah's civil standing in Ephraim, where Kohathite Levites had their cities.

views.label: No; Chronicles built the Levite line

argument.text: Wellhausen argues that the Chronicler drew the Levite pedigree from 1 Samuel 1:1 and 8:2, reasoning that Samuel "must of course have been of Levitical descent, because his mother consecrated him to the service of the sanctuary".

questions.question: How long did Samuel judge Israel?

views.label: About seventeen to nineteen years before Saul

argument.text: Keil estimates about forty years from the victory at Ebenezer to Saul's death, of which seventeen to nineteen were Samuel's judgeship.

views.label: Twelve years alone, eighteen with Saul

argument.text: Josephus gives Samuel twelve years alone after Eli and eighteen together with Saul.

views.label: Forty years in the editor's scheme

argument.text: Moore suggests that the writer of the forty-year scheme gave Samuel a full forty years.

questions.question: How could David and "Samuel the seer" ordain the gatekeepers together (1 Chronicles 9:22), when Samuel died before David reigned?

views.label: The chronicler took the note from his source

argument.text: Keil grants that Samuel died before David's reign, but holds the chronicler took the remark from his authority; David is named first because the arrangement was his.

views.label: A general memory of the time

argument.text: Bertheau held that the note rests on a general recollection that worship was reorganised "in the time of David and Samuel".
